records.name_note: Admissible dedicated pages split on the lead common name. NC State's Common Name(s) list carries two entries, Blue Spruce then Colorado Spruce (alphabetical), and its Description opens 'Blue spruce is a needled evergreen tree in the pine family (Pinaceae).' RHS's page title reads 'Picea pungens | Colorado spruce', its plant-profile common name beneath the H1 is Colorado spruce, and it lists blue spruce and Rocky Mountain spruce under Other common names. Blue Spruce is used as common_name because NC State's dedicated page leads with it both as the first Common Name(s) entry and as its Description opener; RHS's Colorado spruce is recorded here as the alternative. MoBot's page could not be read from this machine, so it was not consulted.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source read lists blue spruce as toxic to cats or dogs, and NC State's page carries no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag. NC State's stated injury hazard is a handling one, the dangerous leaf tips: it is being replaced by Fraser fir due to the dangerous leaf tips that have caused injury to toddlers. Its structured fields also give Appendage: Prickles and Leaf Feel: Prickly. (NC State separately rates its Fire Risk as high flammability.)
unknowns: MoBot's dedicated Picea pungens page (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=284991) could not be read: the host fails TLS certificate verification from this environment, so it contributed no citations and nothing was taken from it.

Only NC State and RHS have fetched dedicated pages for this taxon; Clemson HGIC, PSU, UMD, UGA and UF/IFAS returned no species-specific Picea pungens page (only cultivar, disease or multi-species pages), so none were used.
toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source states cat or dog toxicity; NC State's dangerous leaf tips are recorded only as a handling hazard in toxicity_detail.

is_houseplant is false: NC State frames it as a Perennial, Tree for landscape use (USDA zones 2a-7a) and no admissible source addresses indoor culture. The research record left it null; set at landing.

water_regime left null: NC State says young trees should be kept consistently moist and not allowed to dry out, but that the tree becomes more drought tolerant as it matures and is more drought tolerant than other spruces, so no single regime applies; RHS gives only Moisture: Moist but well-drained as a soil field. No dry-down or day-interval fields are set for an in-ground tree.
soil_drainage set to moderate from NC State (Good Drainage plus prefers rich, moist soil) and RHS (moist but well-drained); the drainage is not fast or sandy.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: RHS gives only the words acid or neutral, and NC State gives no pH field.

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_sun only. NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, but RHS's Position field lists Full sun only, and NC State's prose frames shade as a tolerance (in full sun, although it will tolerate some shade) and says it prefers rich, moist soil in full sunlight; part_shade is therefore not set.

Size uses NC State's Dimensions block (30-60 ft tall, 10-20 ft wide, converted to inches), which matches its prose. RHS gives Max Height Higher than 12 metres (open-ended, no usable bound), describes the tree as to about 15m, and gives Max Spread 4-8 metres (about 157-315 in), a wider band than NC State's; RHS's figures are not used.

chill_damage_f, temperature, humidity, light_fc, fertilizer fields left null: NC State's USDA zone list 2a-7a is a hardiness range, not a damage-onset figure, and its statement that the tree cannot tolerate heat and humidity gives no percentage.
attracts_pollinators and is_edible left null: neither NC State nor RHS has an Attracts field, pollinator tag or edibility statement for this species.
NC State's Tags field mentions Christmas trees as a use, not as an edibility statement.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list for this page carries four entries in alphabetical order, Baltic Whitewood, Common Spruce, European Spruce, Norway Spruce, so Baltic Whitewood comes first in that list; the same page's Description, however, opens with "The Norway spruce". RHS's dedicated Picea abies page title reads 'Picea abies | Norway spruce', and Baltic whitewood appears only in its Other common names list. Norway Spruce is used as the common name because the Description prose and the RHS page both lead with it. The MoBot Plant Finder page for this taxon could not be loaded, so it was not consulted.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source gives a pet or human toxicity statement for Picea abies, and none was imported from other conifers. The NC State page for this species has no Poison block and no Problem for Cats/Dogs tags. Its only statement about eating is under Uses (Ethnobotany): "Herbal teas are made from leafy twigs." No preparation method, steeping time, dose or safety condition is stated.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded in this session (connection error), so no MoBot evidence was used. Clemson HGIC returned 403 and no dedicated Picea abies page was found on Penn State; UF/IFAS was not reachable. Only NC State and RHS were read.

is_houseplant is false: NC State describes a 40 to 60 ft landscape tree for large home landscapes, woodland and meadow (hardy zones 2a-7b), and neither page frames it as a houseplant. The research record left it null; set at landing.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: no admissible source states pet toxicity for Picea abies; none borrowed from other conifers. The only eating-related statement is NC State's 'Herbal teas are made from leafy twigs.', with no preparation times, doses or safety conditions given. is_edible is true on that statement alone; it covers leafy twigs as an herbal tea only, nothing else, and no source addresses safety.

water_regime left null: NC State gives Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage plus Moist and prose 'moderately moist, well-drained', and RHS gives Moisture 'Moist but well-drained'. These are soil-moisture descriptors, not a watering statement. NC State also warns the tree 'dislikes heat, wet feet, and hot, dry summers'.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH is the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', and RHS gives only 'Acid or Neutral' with no numbers.

RHS's structured Max Height and Max Spread are open-ended ('Higher than 12 metres', 'wider than 8 metres'). RHS's description gives a single ceiling, 'to 30m tall' (about 1,181 in), which is far above NC State's cultivated range. mature size comes from NC State's species Dimensions block (Height 40-60 ft = 480-720 in; Width 25-30 ft = 300-360 in), and RHS's 30 m figure is disclosed but not used.

attracts_pollinators left null: NC State's Attracts field lists Small Mammals and Songbirds, its Wildlife Value prose says birds, moths and small mammals are attracted, and the page says the female cones are pollinated by wind-borne pollen. No pollinator-attracting statement was found.

NC State's structured Light field reads 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'. That hour figure is NC State's generic category definition and an open-ended floor, so it gives no ceiling, and the species prose gives no hour figure. direct_sun_hours_max is left null. RHS Position is also Full sun.

Humidity, temperature, indoor light, fertilizing and watering-interval fields are null: no admissible source read gives them for this in-ground tree. No chill-damage onset temperature is stated; hardiness zones 2a-7b (NC State) and RHS H7 are survival ratings, not damage onsets.

Cultivars captured as cultivars of Picea abies only: NC State lists 'Nidiformis' (dwarf with a nest-like depression in its compact mounded habit), 'Pendula' (weeping, 12 to 15 feet tall and wide) and 'Berry Gardens' (dwarf, weeping). Their sizes are not the species' sizes. NC State warns Norway spruce does poorly in zone 7 in the southern US because it prefers cool summers. Picea glauca and Picea pungens are separate species; NC State's 'is often confused with' module lists Picea pungens among others.

records.name_note: NC State lists the former name "Azalea indica" under "Previously known as:", and RHS lists "Azalea indica" among the synonyms of this taxon.
records.toxicity_detail: Two admissible dedicated pages for this exact taxon, with different tones. NC State (Rhododendron indicum): top-of-page statement "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped, separate from the pet tags) reads: Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "While the plants are known to contain toxins, ingestion of moderate amounts of azalea (nectar or leaves) poses little toxic hazard."; Poison Toxic Principle: Grayanotoxins; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice. NC State's Plant Type field lists two values, Poisonous and Shrub. Its Problems field lists Frequent Disease Problems, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. NC State's Poison Symptoms entry names no specific symptom, and the page says nothing about honey. RHS (Rhododendron indicum (EA), Potentially harmful): "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, tortoises) Harmful if eaten - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". The sources differ in tone: NC State rates human hazard low for moderate ingestion of nectar or leaves; RHS says harmful if eaten without that qualification. toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries and RHS's dog- and cat-scoped pets line. The ASPCA listing and any honey/nectar warning are not on an admissible page for this taxon and are not cited.
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page for Rhododendron indicum (taxonid=280025) could not be loaded: every fetch failed with a TLS certificate error, and plantfinder.mobot.org is known to refuse non-browser clients. Nothing is cited from it, and no MoBot-only fields (zone, water, bloom, noteworthy characteristics) were filled.

No dedicated Rhododendron indicum page was found on hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu or fieldreport.caes.uga.edu. Clemson and UGA azalea pages found were genus or group-level and were not used.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries plus RHS's 'Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, tortoises) Harmful if eaten'. The ASPCA listing the task refers to is not an admissible source. No admissible source on these pages states anything about honey; NC State mentions only 'nectar or leaves' in its human-scoped symptom line, and it rates that low hazard for moderate amounts.

is_edible=false rests on RHS 'Harmful if eaten'. NC State's human-scoped line says ingestion of moderate amounts of nectar or leaves poses little toxic hazard, which is softer than RHS. No source describes the plant as a food.

water_regime left null. NC State has 'Moist' as a soil-drainage tag and the description calls the soil 'moist'; RHS has a structured 'Moist but well-drained' Moisture field. These are soil adjectives, not watering instructions. RHS's Cultivation sentence about not letting plants dry out was not checked against sibling azalea pages, so it was not used. No watering statement specific to this taxon was adopted.

soil_drainage=moderate because NC State's Soil Drainage tags are exactly Good Drainage and Moist, and RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained'. Both point to the middle of the scale. NC State also says the plant is intolerant of wet soils and warns of Phytophthora root rot with overwatering, which rules out moisture_retentive.

soil_base=garden_bed is an in-ground classification inferred from the landscape shrub setting. NC State's soil texture is High Organic Matter and Loam (Silt), and RHS's soil types are Clay, Loam, Sand. Neither source names a potting mix.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null. NC State gives 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band, and RHS gives only 'Acid'.

direct_sun_hours_max left null. NC State's 2-6 hours appears only in its site-wide Partial Shade legend text next to the tag, not in species prose. RHS Position is Partial shade, and its Cultivation text says 'partial or dappled shade'.

Size: NC State gives Height 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. and Width 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in., which is 24-36 inches, and this is used as the anchor. RHS gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres, which is 19.7-39.4 inches. RHS also gives Time to Maturity of 5-10 years and says 'to about 1m high' in its description.

NC State's hardiness zones (7a-8b) and RHS's H5 rating are survival or range ratings, not damage-onset temperatures, so chill_damage_f is null. No admissible page for this taxon gives day or night temperatures, humidity, fertilizer interval or strength, or light in foot-candles.

is_houseplant is false: neither page frames this as a houseplant; both treat it as an outdoor shrub (NC State Plant Type Poisonous, Shrub; USDA zones 7a-8b). The research record left it null; set at landing.

NC State's Wildlife Value field names 'Members of the genus Rhododendron' for a specialized bee, which is genus-level and was not used. attracts_pollinators rests on the description sentence about specimens in pollinator gardens where the flowers will attract bees.

Naming: this is Rhododendron indicum on both dedicated pages, titled 'Southern Indian Azalea' by NC State (single Common Name(s) entry and title parenthetical) and 'southern Indian azalea' by RHS (page title). It is a separate taxon from Rhododendron simsii ('Indian Azalea') and from the hybrid group sold as 'Southern Indica azaleas'. No admissible page examined for this taxon mentions the Satsuki name, so that link is not asserted. RHS carries Satsuki Group entries as separate pages. The RHS title carries an '(EA)' tag, which is not part of the name.

records.name_note: The three admissible dedicated pages lead with different common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list carries four entries in alphabetical order, Christmas Holly, Common Holly, English Holly, European Holly, and its Description opens 'English holly is a large, ornamental, flowering, evergreen tree or shrub in the holly family (Aquifoliaceae).' RHS's page title reads 'Ilex aquifolium | common holly' and RHS carries English holly among its Other common names. MoBot gives a single Common Name line of English holly. English holly is the one name present on all three, and it is the name NC State's Description opens with, so it is used.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Problems list for this page carries: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Spines/Thorns, Weedy. Its tags include #poisonous fruits, #poisonous if ingested, #spines, #spiny leaves, #thorns, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #problem for cats. The cat and dog tags are separate from the severity rating: NC State's Poison Severity "Low" sits under its human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans" block, not under the cat/dog tags. That block gives Poison Symptoms "Vomiting, diarrhea, and depression. Leaves and berries are low toxicity and it is only in very large doses that problems are likely to arise. Fruits particularly poisonous to children"; Poison Toxic Principle Saponins; Causes Contact Dermatitis No; Poison Part Fruits. The scope is internally mixed: Poison Part lists only Fruits while the symptoms line mentions leaves and berries as low toxicity. NC State's Edibility line reads "Use caution. Human ingestion of berries can cause minor toxic reaction." RHS says "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." The leaves have marginal spines (NC State Appendage: Spines, Thorns). No admissible source gives a cat- or dog-specific symptom list; the ASPCA 'Holly' entry named in the brief is not an admissible domain and is not used. RHS adds a pets line: 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers'. NC State's page header separately reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.'
unknowns: Invasive status: NC State states the plant has become naturalized in the Pacific Northwest and is on the invasive plant list in Oregon, California and Alaska; MoBot says it has naturalized in the Pacific Northwest and carries an Invasive field link. No schema field holds this, so it is recorded here.

Common name is split three ways across the admissible dedicated pages (Christmas Holly first at NC State, common holly at RHS, English holly at MoBot); English holly is the one common to all three. No UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was used.

toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries. RHS also has a pets line in its Potentially harmful field (fruit not to be eaten), but it is an unscoped 'Pets:' line naming neither cats nor dogs, so it is reproduced in toxicity_detail and does not carry the flag. No admissible source gives a cat- or dog-specific symptom list or a pet-scoped severity. The ASPCA entry is not an admissible domain.

is_edible is false from RHS's "not to be eaten" fruit warning and NC State's poisonous-fruit entries. NC State's Edibility line says human ingestion of berries can cause a minor toxic reaction, and its Poisonous to Humans block rates severity Low. The sources differ in emphasis, but none calls it a food plant.

Soil pH left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The Acid band is open-ended, so it gives no floor, and RHS's pH field lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so its open-ended Alkaline does not confirm NC State's 8.0 ceiling. NC State's prose adds that it can grow in very acidic soils.
water_regime left null: NC State and MoBot give only soil-moisture adjectives (moist, well-drained; MoBot Water: Medium, mid-scale) with no watering statement; both warn against poorly drained soil.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); MoBot says full sun to part shade; RHS lists Full sun and Partial shade. Part_shade is the NC State/MoBot partial-shade reading.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figures are NC State's site-wide light-category legend.

Hardiness: RHS rates H6 (UK conditions) and MoBot says zones 7 to 9, but these are survival ratings, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null. humidity_need left null: NC State's 'humidity intolerant' tag and 'dislikes hot and humid summers' describe outdoor summer climate, not a humidity percentage or indoor need.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's Common Name(s) list carries three entries in alphabetical order, Carolina Cherry Laurel, Carolina Cherry-Laurel, Carolina Laurel Cherry, and its Description opens 'Carolina cherry laurel is a broadleaf evergreen, woody shrub to small tree'. RHS's page title reads 'Prunus caroliniana | Carolina cherry laurel'. UF/IFAS's page H1 reads 'Prunus caroliniana: Cherry-Laurel' and its Common name(s) line lists cherry-laurel first, then Carolina laurelcherry. Carolina Cherry Laurel is used because it leads two of the three reachable dedicated pages and is distinct from Prunus laurocerasus (Cherry Laurel), which NC State's 'Prunus caroliniana is often confused with:' module lists for this species together with two of its cultivars.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox. Under its Poisonous to Humans heading (human-scoped) Poison Severity is High; the page also carries the separate tags Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses (tag list: #poisonous, #problem for cats, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #weedy). Problems field: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. Plant Type: Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Tree. Poison Part: Leaves, Seeds, Stems. Toxic principle: Cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin & prunasin); Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Symptoms: Gasping, weakness, excitement, pupil dilation, spasms, convulsions, coma, respiratory failure. 'Stems, leaves, seeds contain cyanide, particularly toxic in the process of wilting: brick red mucous membranes, panting, shock.' Fruit Description: 'Green fruits are cyanogenic, but immature seeds are not. Ripe fruits are free from cyanide, but their mature seeds are strongly cyanogenic.' UF/IFAS is softer: crushed leaves and green twigs are 'quite bitter and possibly poisonous'. The sources do not use the word twigs for NC State's Stems, and no admissible source gives a dose or a livestock-wide statement beyond NC State's Problem for Horses tag.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (taxonid=286443) and Clemson were not usable: plantfinder.mobot.org / missouribotanicalgarden.org refused the connection from here, and Clemson's only relevant page (HGIC 1069 Laurel) is a multi-species page, so neither supplied any field.
Reclassification: no admissible source reviewed uses Laurocerasus caroliniana; RHS lists Prunus caroliniana with name status Correct, so the Prunus name is kept.
Weedy self-seeding as sourced: NC State says it can become weedy in the landscape due to suckering and self-seeding; UF/IFAS says hundreds of seedlings appear beneath the crown each year.

toxic_to_pets rests on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; its Poison Severity High is under the Poisonous to Humans heading. No admissible page states livestock toxicity beyond the Problem for Horses tag, and 'twigs' appears only in UF/IFAS (hedged as possibly poisonous).

is_edible left null: NC State describes fruit/seed cyanide content but states no food use; the fruit is only noted as eaten by wildlife. is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type is Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Tree (USDA zones 7a-10b), and no admissible source frames it as an indoor plant; UF/IFAS notes only that it can be difficult to grow in containers due to root rot and over-irrigation. The research record left is_houseplant null; set at landing.
outdoor_sun_exposure: UF/IFAS Light requirement 'full sun to full shade' is broader than NC State's structured Full sun and Partial Shade; only NC State's structured values are listed.

Size: UF/IFAS gives Height 25 - 40 feet and Spread 15 - 25 feet, larger than NC State's 15-35 ft by 15-20 ft; NC State's Dimensions block is used. RHS gives no Max Height or Max Spread for this species.

soil_drainage moderate: NC State tags include Occasional Flooding, but UF/IFAS says do not plant in wet, soggy areas and over-irrigating can cause chlorosis and death; moderate is the middle reading, not wet.
soil_ph: NC State lists Acid, Alkaline and Neutral (open-ended bands) and RHS lists acid, alkaline and neutral, so no bounds are set. UF/IFAS says the tree adapts well to soils with high pH.

water_regime null: NC State says established plants have good drought tolerance and prefers moist well-drained soil; UF/IFAS says ample moisture while young, then little or no irrigation. These are not a single watering statement. No sourced watering-interval, chill-damage, humidity, light-level or fertilizer figures.

RHS Foliage 'Deciduous' conflicts with the evergreen description of NC State and UF/IFAS and is not used; RHS Hardiness H6 is not used for chill_damage_f because it is a survival rating, not a damage onset; RHS Cultivation text ('Grow in moderately fertile soil in full sun') is genus-level boilerplate and not used.

records.name_note: Only one admissible source (NC State) could be read. Its Common Name(s) list gives Japanese False-cypress first and Sawara False-cypress second (alphabetical); its description prose opens 'The Sawara false-cypress is a large evergreen conifer native to Japan'. Sawara False-cypress is used as common_name on that prose opener, which is not what the list leads with: it is a deliberate choice, and Japanese False-cypress, the list's first entry, is recorded here as the alternative. NC State's C. obtusa page lists only Hinoki Cypress and Hinoki False-cypress, so NC State does not apply Japanese False-cypress to the sibling (landed separately as Hinoki Cypress). NC State lists 'Golden Mop', 'Boulevard', 'Filifera', 'Plumosa Aurea' and 'Squarrosa' under this species' Cultivars / Varieties, so they are cultivars of C. pisifera, not separate entries.
unknowns: Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu could be read. plantfinder.mobot.org failed TLS certificate verification, hgic.clemson.edu returned 403, the RHS species page URL returned 404 and RHS search showed no page for this exact name, and ask.ifas.ufl.edu was blocked by the sandbox. So there is no MoBot, RHS, UF/IFAS or Clemson evidence.

The task brief says NC State applies 'Japanese False-cypress' to C. obtusa too; NC State's C. obtusa page lists Hinoki Cypress and Hinoki False-cypress instead. The Japanese False-cypress overlap was not confirmed on that page.

mature_height_in 600-840 and mature_spread_in 36-240 come from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 50-70 ft, Width 3-20 ft). The same page's description says the cultivated form matures to 20 to 30 feet tall, and most plants sold are compact cultivars, so the block overstates garden size.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours direct sun); Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. The description says 'full sun to part shade'.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the first two are open-ended.
water_regime is null: NC State gives only the soil adjective 'moist but well-drained' and a drought-tolerance trait, which are not a watering statement.
soil_base garden_bed is a classification for an in-ground tree or shrub, supported by the 'moist but well-drained soil' sentence. The sources do not name it.

Not addressed by NC State: pet toxicity, edibility, pollinators, heat limits, fertilizing, humidity; all left null. NC State gives USDA Plant Hardiness Zones 4a-8b, but that is a survival range, not a chill-damage onset, so chill_damage_f is null. NC State does not discuss indoor culture; is_houseplant is set false from its outdoor Plant Type (Shrub, Tree) and zone range.
The brief also asks to keep C. thyoides separate. NC State lists it as a native alternative; no claim here depends on it.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b121 (home-landscape shrubs, hedges, conifers and small trees) landed by repair script scripts/catalog/pipeline/b121_repair.py from the post-audit records. Eight species: Blue Spruce, Norway Spruce, Southern Indian Azalea, English Holly, Bridal Wreath, Sweet Viburnum, Carolina Cherry Laurel, Sawara False-cypress. Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim where given; every substitute quote ground-truthed with qc.py/b121_qc.py first. Landing decisions: no NC State page-title parenthetical is quoted (<title>-only metadata) -- each was replaced by the rendered Common Name(s) list (newline-stacked or one item per quote) or the Description opener; bare RHS 'Correct' kept only in the CORR form beside an RHS page-title/H1 citation naming the taxon (Ilex aquifolium's label-glued 'Name Status Correct' cut to that form); no MoBot citation added (MoBot refuses this machine); RHS label+value quotes cut to the value. Blue Spruce: part_shade dropped per audit (RHS Position lists Full sun only, NC State prose frames shade as a tolerance), toxicity_detail restored with the audit's 'dangerous leaf tips' wording, name_note re-grounded on NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list and Description. English Holly: toxicity_detail restored with RHS's pets line and NC State's banner appended; that RHS 'Pets:' line names neither cats nor dogs, so it is not counted for toxic_to_pets; Ilex opaca / Ilex x meserveae sentences dropped from name_note (only bare <dt> labels were quotable) and disclosed in unknowns. Toxic species (Southern Indian Azalea, English Holly, Carolina Cherry Laurel) cite their full stacked Problems field for the flag and the page's contiguous Poison block for the detail. Spiraea prunifolia lands as Bridal Wreath (title-cased); the b89 hybrid Spiraea x vanhouttei is Vanhoutte Spirea, so no collision, and name_note discloses that NC State lists the two as commonly confused. Sawara False-cypress kept on NC State's Description opener against the audit's Japanese False-cypress (the alphabetized list's first entry), disclosed in name_note and unknowns. is_houseplant null -> false (with Plant Type / zone / landscape-use citations) for the six landscape species the research left null. verify_quotes: MoBot citations the researcher kept on English Holly SKIP.
